## Summary
- The paper introduces TusoAI, an LLM agent for developing computational methods for domain-specific scientific tasks. They apply it to several biological and deep learning problems and demonstrate improvement over other agentic and LLM models. They also demonstrate its performance on iterating on existing state-of-the-art methods and show new scientific insights.

## Recommendation
- Reject. While results comparing with other agentic models are there, the actual performance isn't that much better compared to existing models on the specific tasks. The most interesting result is the case studies, but the other models were not run on the same case studies. There is a lack of case studies in other domains. Code is poorly written and not amenable to open source.

## Weaknesses
- TusoAI is designed to work with any domain as long as domain knowledge is provided, however, there is a strong focus on biological applications. This paper would benefit from showing TusoAI's performance in other scientific domains similar to the two biological case studies. I see that it worked on deep learning but only a cold start was performed. I am specifically asking for a warm start case study in a non-biology domain.
- Diversity in methods produced is a core architecture consideration, but it is not substantiated in the text. While evidence is provided that TusoAI writes diverse code, there are no references supporting the assumption that generating more diverse code is better.
- Code is poorly written / formatted.

## Questions
- Was an ablation study performed on the number of points saved for each paper's methods in Step 1 "Gather domain knowledge"? How does increasing/ descresing point summaries affect the final model performance?
- Why were other models not tested on the case studies? A lot seems to be riding on TusoAI's new findings, but other models were not given a chance.
- How is the iterative refinement done for "The initialization agent Ainit drafts 5 candidate solution descriptions from T and iteratively refines them using each paper summary in P"? It is not clear and appears to be super important.
- How many hyperparameters are there total for this agent? It appears to have a lot, and I would be curious how those hyperparameters affect the solutions. (ie. run time, integer values used in various places, utility scalars, probabilities, bug-fix attempts, etc..)
- Which hardware is used for all of this? 8 hours means a totally different thing on a laptop vs. a data center. Are all models tested on the same hardware? I see some models are only accessible on the web: how do you account for different compute capabilities?
- How many runs were used for ablation analysis (Table 3)? Was it just run once, or several times with mean score? If it was run once then it needs to be run more times, since LLMs are very stochastic and the results can vary significantly.
- Where is the conclusion/future work section? The paper seems to end abruptly.

## Feedback
- The code is a mess. There are import statements all over the place, comments are unstructured and lacking in many places, and there are no clear instructions on how to reproduce results. Please fix this so I can take a look at the code myself and run things locally.
- I_{diag} is not updated in Algorithm 1, it appears to remain as an empty list. Please consider removing or correct this.

Thank you for noting the usefulness of TusoAI and for providing detailed comments that helped us substantially improve the manuscript. We address each of the reviewer’s points below. The manuscript has been revised accordingly, incorporating 10 new analyses and updates to 3 main figures, and 13 supplementary sections. Before proceeding to the point-by-point responses, we briefly address the reviewer’s 4 high-level concerns:

(i) TusoAI did not significantly outperform existing models. 

We agree that the improvements on the tasks are moderate rather than dramatic. This outcome is largely driven by the nature of these problems, which differ substantially from typical ML-agent benchmarks (e.g., Kaggle, MLE-Bench). Many of our tasks—such as scRNA-seq denoising and cell-type deconvolution—are highly specialized scientific workflows that have been iteratively optimized by domain experts over many years [1]. We emphasize that in such settings, even modest gains over strong human-engineered baselines are uncommon, and our improvements to scientific tasks are comparable or even greater than the improvements that led to expert methods being published. See examples below:

In the original scDRS paper Figure 2 (corresponding to our Figure 3), the authors report a 20-30% power improvement over the strongest baseline in causal simulations, whereas we discover a 40% improvement over scDRS.  In the original pgBoost paper Figure 3 (corresponding to our Figure 4), the authors report a 5-8% enrichment improvement over the strongest baseline, whereas we discover a further 7-14% improvement over pgBoost. This improvement is particularly large at distal links (emphasized in pgBoost as a very important case), where our enrichment is double that of pgBoost. 
Agentic optimization work by Aygun et al reports similarly modest gains, in Figure 2 of their paper they improve a single cell task from 0.5 to 0.6 and an expert deep learning model from 0.76 to 0.82, without comparing to NAS methods. Agentic optimization work for biology BioML bench finds that agentic approaches (such as AIDE or Biomni) often struggle to meet expert baselines, let alone outperform them. We show TusoAI can often outperform expert methods, both from scratch and by improving upon existing work.
Deep learning tasks have been historically more difficult for agentic approaches and not the main focus (AIDE did not consider deep learning originally, AutoML-Agent does not outperform AutoML and humans in their deep learning tasks, CellForge is an agentic approach that does not outperform human deep learning models). This is replicated in our deep learning analysis where AIDE has an average rank of 9.8. In contrast, TusoAI is the top ranked (Avg. Rank 2.8) among all methods (including experts and AutoML). Thus, TusoAI being the top performing agentic NAS method, at least as good as the top performing NAS method, and meeting or outperforming human experts in 3 out of 5 deep learning tasks is indeed an important advance for agentic optimization performance.

[1] M. D. Luecken, S. Gigante, D. B. Burkhardt, et al. Defining and benchmarking open problems in single-cell analysis. Nature Biotechnology

(ii) Other models not run on case studies. 

For the two case studies (scDRS and pgBoost), we compared only against the original human-designed methods rather than other agentic baselines because these methods have large, specialized codebases that TusoAI can directly build upon, whereas other agentic baselines would require full code re-implementation, which is not practical. Optimizing existing methods is a core consideration of TusoAI, but less explored in related work. Additional details are provided in our response to below. 

(iii) Lack of case studies in other domains.

We focused our case studies on genetics for two reasons. First, these problems—detecting disease-critical cell populations and linking variants to target genes—are among the most complex and high-impact problems in human genetics and are central to understanding disease mechanisms and therapeutic development (Lappalainen 2021 Science; Song 2025 Nature; Zhang 2022 Nat Genet; Dorans 2025 Nat Genet; Sakaue 2024 Nat Genet). Second, our goal was to demonstrate depth rather than breadth: each case study is a full scientific analysis in which TusoAI improves state-of-the-art methods (scDRS, pgBoost), uncovers additional biologically plausible findings, and yields ready-to-use implementations that would typically take years to develop manually. We acknowledge that our empirical focus is narrower in domain, and we clarify that although our evaluation centers on genomics and genetics due to their complexity and relevance, TusoAI is designed as a general framework applicable to other scientific domains (line 536).

kn4q-W1: Discussion and conclusion. 

Thank you for this comment. We have added a new Discussion section summarizing the main conclusions, limitations, and directions for future work at Section 6, as shown below:

“We acknowledge several limitations and areas for future work. TusoAI requires a separate validation experiment to base optimization on to prevent overfitting. This experiment should also be quick to run while representing final performance. When optimizing an existing method, TusoAI performs strongest when most of the method is in a single function, and may not perform well if the method is scattered throughout a large codebase. TusoAI does not consider making new evaluation procedures, but rather relies on existing ones and will be vulnerable to the same weaknesses those may have. Several algorithm components are heuristic and may benefit from theoretic justification. We generally focus on biological applications given their complexity and relevance, but achieve reliable performance in diverse scientific domains. Future work may include processing multiple functions in parallel by treating them as separate subtasks, or searching over not just the code-space for methods, but also the data-space for additional useful data to include in a method, as is common in scientific domains.”


>the Bayesian update step is unclear and not described

kn4q-W2: Details for the Bayesian update. 

Thank you for the question. We recognize that it is our responsibility to provide a clear exposition. The Bayesian update in TusoAI corresponds to lines 2, 8, and 9 of Algorithm 1. Each instruction category c is initialized with a prior probability c (line 2). At each iteration, a category is sampled according to these probabilities (line 8), and if the resulting instruction produces an improved solution, its probability is updated multiplicatively to c1.1c (line 9). We have updated lines 257-259 to clarify these points. 

We also provide additional rationale for this design. The Bayesian update step serves as a heuristic that mimics how a scientist might prioritize among several categories of actions (e.g., refining preprocessing, revisiting modeling assumptions, or modifying optimization strategies). The update increases the likelihood of selecting categories that have previously led to performance improvements, thereby implementing an implicit optimization over expected performance gain. Alternatively, a fully formalized optimization formulation could yield a more principled Bayesian update procedure. For instance, one could adopt a Thompson Sampling-style formulation in which each category is associated with a reward probability pc governed by a Beta prior, and at each iteration the category with the largest sampled value is selected. We have clarified this interpretation and discussed this limitation in Section 6 (line 535).

kn4q-W3: Justification of the method. 

Thank you for the comment. We agree that TusoAI is largely heuristic and that proper justification of its components is important. While providing a rigorous theoretical analysis for agentic systems remains challenging—largely due to the complex interactions among LLM reasoning, external tools, stochastic sampling, and iterative feedback loops—we justify our design through empirical evidence and high-level reasoning.

First, our ablation studies demonstrate that each key component of TusoAI—the knowledge-tree structure, the Bayesian update mechanism, and the diagnosis-based optimization—contributes independently to performance improvements (Table 3). This provides empirical support for the necessity of these design choices.

Second, we provide the high-level intuitions guiding the design of TusoAI, which aims to mimic how human scientists iteratively develop computational methods:

(i) Knowledge tree & categorical structure: This reframes the optimization problem from “improve the model” to “improve the model by doing X”. This hierarchical structure provides guidance for the optimization process, analogous to how few-shot prompting provides additional structure compared to zero-shot prompting.

(ii) Bayesian update: If a scientist tries an idea from a particular conceptual category (e.g., preprocessing) and observes improved performance, they are more likely to revisit that category. The Bayesian update encodes this intuition by increasing the probability of selecting successful categories.

(iii) Diagnosis-based optimization: As a model evolves, new diagnostic information becomes available (e.g., intermediate representations or residual patterns). Reviewing such signals closely resembles how scientists debug or refine methods beyond simply reprinting original metrics.

We have updated Section 1(lines 62), Section 3 (lines 267-269), and Section 6 (line 535) to clarify these points and explicitly discuss the heuristic nature and limitations of the approach.

Task description: “build a classification model”
Dataset: “simulated X and Y”
Evaluator: “accuracy on held out validation split”

Line 1: TusoAI retrieves and summarizes 10 highly cited papers relevant to the task.

Line 3: Initialize solutions. TusoAI generates 5 initial solutions, such as logistic regression or random forest. 

Lines 4-15: Iterations. TusoAI selects instructions across categories to iteratively refine the solutions, allocating ~80% of iterations to optimization instructions (lines 8–10) and ~20% to diagnostic instructions (lines 11–13). During Bayesian updates (line 9), TusoAI initially assigns high utility to category preprocessing ($\pi_c=0.6$, time=0 hours), then shifts focus to category regularization ($\pi_c=0.5$, time=2 hours), and finally prioritizes category hyperparameter tuning ($\pi_c=0.5$, time=4 hours).

>Regarding the update rule: Have you considered a robustness or sensitivity analysis comparing the Bayesian update to alternative heuristic updates? More fundamentally, what is the core justification for choosing a Bayesian-style formulation in the first place?

kn4q-R1-Q2: Bayesian update. 

Thank you for the comment. The reviewer raised 2 questions: (i) robustness or sensitivity analysis comparing the Bayesian update to alternative heuristic updates, and (ii) core justification for choosing a Bayesian-style formulation. We first summarize the Bayesian update and then address each question in turn. 

The Bayesian update: TusoAI groups instructions into categories (e.g., a “regularization” category containing “L1 loss, L2 loss” and a “preprocessing” category containing “normalization, log scaling”). Each category is assigned an initial category-specific probability (line 2). In each iteration, TusoAI samples a category (line 8), selects an instruction from the category, and—if the resulting solution improves performance—increases the probability of that category via a multiplicative update (line 9).

(i) Robustness or sensitivity analysis comparing the Bayesian update to alternative heuristic updates. 

We compared the default Bayesian-style update against a simple heuristic baseline that samples categories uniformly throughout all iterations (TusoAI - No Bayesian) and an even simpler heuristic baseline that samples instructions uniformly throughout all iterations (TusoAI - No Categories). This isolates the contribution of the Bayesian update over the categorical structure. As shown in Table 3 of the original submission, the Bayesian update yields substantially higher performance (average score 0.66 vs. 0.55 and 0.57, resp.). We clarified this in Section 4.2 (lines 401–402).

(ii) Core justification for Bayesian-style formulation. 

We recognize that it is our responsibility to provide a clear exposition. We have expanded our previous response to kn4q-W3 to provide more clear justification. First, the design reflects how scientists typically develop computational methods: they reason at the level of broad categories—such as preprocessing, modeling, or regularization—and tend to revisit categories that previously led to improvements. This motivates assigning probabilities at the category level rather than the instruction level. Second, the multiplicative update provides a soft mechanism for incorporating evidence: a successful improvement slightly increases the likelihood that the same category will be sampled again. A more formal alternative would be a bandit-style update (e.g., Thompson Sampling with a Beta prior for each category’s success probability $\pi_c$), but we opted for the simpler constant–multiplicative rule because it is easy to interpret and performs well in practice. We have clarified this interpretation and discussed this limitation in Section 6 (line 535).

strengths.value:
1) Mixing Bayesian optimization in the loop of an agentic AI system is interesting. I wish the paper had substantiated whether this is the first agent of this type or whether the idea is inspired by existing agents. 

2) The results show that some of the methods constructed by TusoAI are novel rather than simple re-implementation of existing approaches or calls to standard packages.

3) The agentic system is tested in many scenarios, from final performance to behavior over time.

4) Single-cell results show promising biological results.

weaknesses.value:
1) The writing can be improved. For example, the Abstract is excessively long. Instead of listing all results, please summarize the key points and condense the Abstract's opening.

2) While the evaluations involve tasks beyond a single cell, it seems like TusoAI's performance is more pronounced in the single cell case, which might suggest the paper could have made that the central focus rather than a general-purpose multi-agent AI.

3) The code is not available for a full review of the paper.

4) Narrow scope to problems that can be solved using off-the-shelf ML models and strategies rather than those that need in-depth model development (e.g., new deep learning models rather than say fine-tuning Restnet). 

5) As discussed in the *LLM-based general learning agents* section, there are already agents developed for ML engineering. This work differentiates itself from those by focusing on scientific domains, but some baselines are still missing (R&D, DS, etc).

6) Limitation in scale: only 10 papers retrieved from Semantic Scholar.

7) I have some concerns about model selection and evaluation, which I have asked in the box below.

questions.value:

4)  Does increasing the number of papers retrieved from Semantics Scholar (from 10) improve the results?
